clue.text: Forward-looking Browning seems to favour what's piquant

parts.note: to be pro something is to favour it
spice is what gives food a piquant taste

explanation.surface: A remark that the poet Browning seems to like sharp, spicy flavours.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Browning wrote a poem whose Latin title means 'look forward'; 'Forward-looking' translates that title, so the definition names the poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Browning's poem about facing death bravely carries a Latin title meaning 'look ahead'.

clue.text: The bony flag-man makes good speed

parts.note: PI, short for pious, means good
a rate is a speed of going

explanation.surface: A signal-man with a skeletal flag who moves along quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'bony flag' is the skull and crossbones of the Jolly Roger.
explanation.definitionFit: A buccaneer sails under the skull-and-crossbones flag.

clue.text: It's work to a standstill, let's face it !

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
a pose is a held, motionless position

explanation.surface: A remark that work has ground to a halt, with an invitation to accept it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'face it' looks like 'accept it'; 'face' is to confront or resist.
explanation.definitionFit: To oppose someone is to confront or stand against them.

clue.text: Carried out by the class, Edward ?

parts.note: per means by, as in per post
a form is a class in a British school
Ed is short for Edward

explanation.surface: Asking whether the schoolchildren did something, Edward.
explanation.definitionFit: Performed means executed or done, a task carried through.

clue.text: Taking the medium view ?

parts.note: a moderate opinion is reread as the sight possessed by a spiritualist medium

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone holds a moderate opinion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'medium' suggests middle-of-the-road; here it is a psychic who sees the future.
explanation.definitionFit: Clairvoyance is the supposed power of seeing beyond the senses, a medium's gift.

clue.text: Half a hookah makes such a row !

indicators.note: only the front half of each word of the hookah's two-part name is kept

parts.note: a hubble-bubble is a hookah, a water pipe for smoking
a hubble-bubble is a hookah, a water pipe for smoking

explanation.surface: Someone notes that even a half-smoked water pipe causes a commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: The hookah is a hubble-bubble; 'Half' keeps the front half of each of its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A hubbub is a noisy din, the kind of loud racket a row produces.

clue.text: From this realm take a south-easterly direction

parts.note: this realm is the United Kingdom, abbreviated UK
SE is the compass abbreviation for south-east

explanation.surface: Instructions to leave the country heading south-east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'direction' looks like a compass bearing; it is an order.
explanation.definitionFit: A ukase was a decree from the Russian Tsar, an official order or command.

clue.text: Unadorned pie for Uncle Ned

parts.note: bald means plain and unadorned, as in a bald statement
pâté was the French word for a pie or pastry

explanation.surface: Serving a plain pie to an uncle.
explanation.walkthrough: In the old song 'Uncle Ned' had 'no hair on the top of his head'.
explanation.definitionFit: A baldpate is a person with a hairless head, as the song's Uncle Ned was.

clue.text: "Finis " expressed in hold-ups ?

parts.note: the word printed at a book's close is read as the end of a book, and hold-ups are supports keeping volumes upright

explanation.surface: Asking whether 'the end' is announced during robberies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hold-ups' sound like robberies; they are supports that keep books standing.
explanation.definitionFit: Bookends are the supports at each end of a shelf row, literally the ends of the books.

clue.text: Mixed pair in slanting rain on the bank

indicators.note: one jumbled word goes inside the other
rain that slants is knocked askew, so its letters are rearranged too
the letters of pair are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A couple caught in driving, slanting rain beside a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slanting' looks like it describes the weather, but it is a second anagram signal; 'in' places one jumbled word inside the other, just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Riparian is the adjective for things living or situated beside a river, that is, on its bank.

clue.text: Last trump from a huntsman ?

parts.note: the final trumpet blast of Judgment Day is recast as the shout a hunter gives to urge on the hounds

explanation.surface: Wondering what a huntsman's final trumpet call would be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last trump' suggests the trumpet at the end of the world; here it is just the huntsman's final cry at the chase.
explanation.definitionFit: A halloo is the shout used in hunting to encourage hounds, a huntsman's call.

clue.text: Plain but imposing Russians ?

parts.note: Russians from the elevated grassy plains of their country, also showy horses

explanation.surface: Describing some Russians as homely yet impressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' looks like homely; it is the steppe, the Russian grassland, so people of the high steppes.
explanation.definitionFit: High-steppers are horses that lift their feet high, and so people of stately bearing.

clue.text: The agency has nothing for the poet

parts.note: TASS was the official Soviet news agency
O, the round zero, means nothing

explanation.surface: A news bureau that has nothing to offer a poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Torquato Tasso was the Italian Renaissance poet who wrote Jerusalem Delivered.

clue.text: Hot spot for two dozen flighty choristers !

definitions.text: Hot spot for two dozen flighty choristers !

parts.words: Hot spot for two dozen flighty choristers !
parts.note: the nursery rhyme's four and twenty singing blackbirds were baked in a pastry dish, the warm place they ended up

explanation.surface: A warm venue booked for a choir of twenty-four skittish singers.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'choristers' are the four-and-twenty blackbirds of 'Sing a Song of Sixpence', which were baked in a pie and began to sing when it was opened.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised pie is a tall pastry pie with stiff sides, like the dish the rhyme's blackbirds were baked in.

clue.text: Unlike the shaggy dog

parts.note: a dog that is not shaggy has a sleek, short fur

explanation.surface: Contrasting some animal with a shaggy dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Smooth-coated describes an animal with short sleek fur, the opposite of a shaggy one.

clue.text: Perhaps probe into the "false pretences" offence

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters are only one possible arrangement, so they are shuffled

explanation.surface: Suggesting an investigation into a charge of fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges PROBE and INTO together.
explanation.definitionFit: Obreption is the legal term for obtaining something by false statement, a fraud.

clue.text: Evades the long arm of the law

definitions.text: Evades the long arm of the law

parts.words: Evades the long arm of the law
parts.note: slipping away beyond the reach of the police

explanation.surface: Someone avoiding capture by the police.
explanation.definitionFit: To abscond is to flee secretly to avoid arrest or justice.

clue.text: A striking association

parts.note: a striking implement and a society, or a society of those who strike a ball

explanation.surface: Describing a memorable link between two things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'striking' looks like remarkable; it is hitting a ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A golf club is both the stick used to hit the ball and the society of players.

clue.text: Is theirs " the babbling gossip of the air " ?

definitions.text: Is theirs " the babbling gossip of the air " ?

parts.words: Is theirs " the babbling gossip of the air " ?
parts.note: a line from Twelfth Night about chattering on the air is applied to people who talk over the radio waves

explanation.surface: Asking whose is the chattering of the air in a famous quotation.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrase is Viola's in Twelfth Night; 'the air' here means the airwaves of radio.
explanation.definitionFit: Broadcasters are radio and television presenters, whose talk goes out over the air.

clue.text: Such a welcome for Leander !

parts.note: in Greek myth Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to his lover, so her greeting is named after her

explanation.surface: Praising the greeting given to someone called Leander.
explanation.walkthrough: Leander's lover was Hero, priestess at Sestos, so a welcome 'Hero-ic' in her manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroic means grand and courageous; split as a pun it means like Hero, his lover.

clue.text: Donkey swallows a swan; no wonder they're quivering !

indicators.note: the donkey swallows the swan, so the bird goes inside the animal

parts.note: an ass is a donkey
a pen is a female swan

explanation.surface: A donkey gulps down a swan, so of course things tremble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no wonder' is a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspen leaves tremble in the faintest breeze; the quaking aspen is named for this.

clue.text: Wherein J. Alfred Prufrock presumably made quite a stir!

definitions.text: Wherein J. Alfred Prufrock presumably made quite a stir!

parts.words: Wherein J. Alfred Prufrock presumably made quite a stir!
parts.note: Eliot's Prufrock measured out his life with coffee spoons, so the stir he made was with a spoon in a vessel

explanation.surface: Wondering where T. S. Eliot's timid Prufrock ever caused a sensation.
explanation.walkthrough: In Eliot's poem Prufrock says 'I have measured out my life with coffee spoons'; 'made quite a stir' is literal stirring, not causing a sensation.
explanation.definitionFit: A coffee cup is the drinking vessel in which a coffee spoon stirs.

clue.text: Call up the dark girl with a good heart

indicators.note: good is put at the heart of the girl, in her middle

parts.note: Eve is a girl's name, and eve also means evening, the dark part of the day
OK means good or all right

explanation.surface: Telephoning the dark-haired girl who has a kind heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dark girl' suggests a brunette; it is Eve, whose name is also the evening.
explanation.definitionFit: To evoke is to summon a memory or feeling, to bring it to mind.

clue.text: The Fleet Street crowd

definitions.meaning: London's Fleet Street was the home of the national newspapers, so it stands for the newspaper world
to crowd is to push or squeeze, as a throng does

explanation.surface: Describing the journalists who gather on London's newspaper street.
explanation.definitionFit: The press is the newspaper trade once centred on Fleet Street, and to press is to crowd or squeeze in.

clue.text: The Admiral in the hold ? Lord !

definitions.meaning: Horatio ... was Britain's most famous admiral, victor at Trafalgar
a wrestling hold, an arm lock applied from behind

explanation.surface: An exclamation at finding an admiral down in a ship's cargo space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hold' is not the ship's hold but a wrestling grip; 'Lord' nods to Lord Nelson's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Admiral Lord Nelson shares a name with the wrestling grip in which the arms lock behind an opponent's neck.

clue.text: One's time is taken up in the short interval

indicators.note: the words are taken up and rearranged into a new order

parts.note: the word read with its S as a letter

explanation.surface: Someone complains that their time gets eaten up in a brief break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is taken up' rearranges ONES and TIME together.
explanation.definitionFit: A semitone is the smallest step in Western music, half a whole tone, so a short musical interval.

clue.text: Furs for Hamlet's suit

definitions.meaning: sable is the dark fur of a small Siberian animal
Hamlet says he will wear a suit of ..., meaning mourning black

explanation.surface: Choosing furs to make a costume for Hamlet.
explanation.definitionFit: Sables are costly dark furs, and in heraldry and Shakespeare sable means black, the colour of Hamlet's mourning clothes.

clue.text: Donkeymen in Shakespeare, as in one island ?

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
Cos is a Greek island in the Dodecanese

explanation.surface: Asking whether Shakespeare's donkey-handlers lived together on one island.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare uses 'asinico' (a little ass, a fool) in Troilus and Cressida.
explanation.definitionFit: An asinico is Shakespeare's word for a fool or dolt, literally a little donkey.
